question: A 4-week-old newborn is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. He was born at 40 weeks' gestation and weighed 3300 g (7 lb 4 oz). He now weighs 4300 g (9 lbs 1 oz). There is no family history of serious illness. He is at the 50th percentile for height and 50th percentile for weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a grade 3/6 harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and a soft mid-diastolic murmur over the cardiac apex. The lungs are clear to auscultation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's physical findings?

options.opa: Communication between the pulmonary artery and the thoracic aorta
options.opb: Right-to-left shunt through the atrial septum
options.opc: Left-to-right shunt through the ventricular septum
options.ope: Right-to-left shunt through the ventricular septum

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Grade 3/6 harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border" -> "Possible ventricular septal defect" -> "Left-to-right shunt through the ventricular septum" -> 80% CHAIN: "Soft mid-diastolic murmur over the cardiac apex" -> "Possible mitral valve regurgitation" -> "Left-to-right shunt through the ventricular septum" -> 75% CHAIN: "Weight gain from 3300 g to 4300 g in a 4-week-old newborn" -> "Normal growth" -> "Less likely to be due to right ventricular outflow obstruction" -> 80%
analysis: The physical findings of a grade 3/6 harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and a soft mid-diastolic murmur over the cardiac apex are suggestive of a ventricular septal defect (VSD). VSD is a common congenital heart defect that results in a left-to-right shunt between the ventricles, leading to the characteristic murmurs heard on auscultation.
